clinical: Peritonitis

Peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum, the serosa that covers the bowel. It follows bowel perforation or spreading infection and causes severe abdominal pain and tenderness, and it usually needs urgent treatment.
Adhesions
Fibrous bands can form between serosal surfaces after abdominal surgery or infection. They can twist or block the small bowel, causing obstruction.
Anastomotic leak
Surgeons place sutures through the submucosa at a bowel join (an anastomosis) because it is the strongest layer and holds stitches best. A leak at that join is a serious complication.
Coeliac disease
In coeliac disease, an immune reaction to gluten fills the lamina propria with lymphocytes and plasma cells, and the villi flatten. Absorption falls, causing weight loss, diarrhoea and anaemia.
Hirschsprung disease

In Hirschsprung disease, the myenteric and submucosal plexuses fail to form in a segment of bowel, so that segment stays constricted and the bowel above it swells. It usually presents in newborns who fail to pass meconium.
Mesenteric ischaemia

The ileum is fed by branches of the superior mesenteric artery. If that artery is blocked, for example by a clot, the bowel can lose its blood supply, causing severe pain and tissue death if not treated quickly.

Villi.description: Each villus is a finger-like fold of the mucosa that greatly increases the surface area for absorption. Its core holds loose connective tissue, a central lacteal that takes up dietary fat as chylomicrons, and a fenestrated capillary network that absorbs sugars and amino acids. Strands of smooth muscle run up the core and shorten the villus, squeezing fat-rich lymph out of the lacteal.
clinical: Intestinal lymphangiectasia

Dilated or blocked lacteals let lymph and protein leak into the bowel, causing protein loss, low blood albumin and swelling of the legs. Dietary fat is also poorly absorbed because it cannot leave the villus normally.

Lymphoid cellular regions.description: Peyer's patches are clusters of lymphoid follicles in the ileal wall that help defend the gut against swallowed microbes. Active follicles contain a germinal centre, where B cells multiply and mature into IgA-producing cells, surrounded by a mantle of small lymphocytes. The subepithelial dome sits just under the lining, where specialised M cells carry antigens from the gut lumen to immune cells.
clinical: Typhoid fever
Salmonella Typhi invades the Peyer's patches, which swell, then die and ulcerate, mostly in the second and third weeks of infection. The ulcers can perforate the terminal ileum, causing peritonitis.
Crohn disease
Crohn disease often affects the terminal ileum. Its earliest lesions are small aphthous ulcers that form over lymphoid follicles such as Peyer's patches.

Cellular epithelium.description: The ileum's lining is a single layer of tall cells, mostly absorptive enterocytes whose microvilli form a brush border. Goblet cells on the villi make protective mucus, and Paneth cells at the base of the crypts release antimicrobial substances. Stem cells in the crypts replace the whole lining about every few days.
clinical: Rotavirus infection
Rotavirus infects the enterocytes near the villus tips, destroying them. This shortens the villi and causes watery diarrhoea, mainly in young children.
Lactose intolerance
Enterocytes make lactase, the brush-border enzyme that splits milk sugar. When lactase is low, undigested lactose is fermented in the colon, causing bloating, gas and diarrhoea.

parts.description: The outer longitudinal layer is the thinner, outer sheet of smooth muscle in the muscularis externa, running lengthwise along the gut between the serosa and the myenteric plexus. Its contraction shortens the bowel segment, and working with the inner circular layer it drives peristalsis and segmentation. In a section, it is recognised by bundles of smooth muscle cells cut lengthwise, with long, spindle-shaped nuclei, whereas the circular layer is cut across.

The inner circular layer is the thicker inner sheet of smooth muscle in the muscularis externa, wrapped around the gut inside the myenteric plexus. Its contraction narrows the lumen and, with the outer layer, propels food along the tube. The layer thickens at several sites to form the pyloric and internal anal sphincters and the ileocaecal sphincter. In a section, it is cut across, so its nuclei look round, whereas the outer longitudinal layer is cut lengthwise.

The submucosa is a layer of dense irregular connective tissue lying between the muscularis mucosae and the inner circular muscle layer. It carries the larger arterioles, venules and lymphatics, together with the submucosal (Meissner) plexus, and gives the wall its strength, which is why it holds sutures well. In a section, it appears as a collagen-rich layer stained pink with eosin, containing blood vessels and small nerve ganglia.

Submucosal arterioles are small muscular arteries in the submucosa, the layer beneath the muscularis mucosae, that branch from the vasa recta, the straight vessels that supply the gut wall from the mesentery. They form a network within the submucosa, and from it smaller branches pierce the muscularis mucosae to feed the capillaries of the crypts and villi. In a section, they show a thick smooth-muscle wall around a small lumen, which separates them from the thin-walled venules beside them.

Submucosal venules are the small, thin-walled veins of the submucosa that collect blood from the mucosal capillaries and join larger submucosal veins. Their walls are much thinner than those of the neighbouring arterioles, and their lumens are wider, which helps identify them in a section. The blood they carry is rich in nutrients absorbed from the gut, and it drains through the superior mesenteric vein to the hepatic portal vein and the liver.

Mucosal branches are the small arterioles and venules that pass upward through the muscularis mucosae, linking the submucosal vessels with the mucosa. Arterioles carry blood up to the capillary networks of the lamina propria and villi, and venules return it to the submucosa. In a section, look for small vessels crossing the thin muscularis mucosae between the submucosa and the crypts and villi.

Submucosal lymphatic collectors are the larger lymphatic vessels of the submucosa, lying alongside the blood vessels and the submucosal plexus. They gather lymph from the lacteals of the villi and from the lymphatic plexus of the mucosa, and carry it, often rich in fat as chylomicrons, towards the mesenteric lymph nodes. Their thin walls and pale contents, which hold lymph rather than red blood cells, help identify them in a section.

The lamina propria is the loose, areolar connective tissue of the mucosa, lying between the epithelium and the muscularis mucosae and filling the spaces between the crypts. It contains IgA-secreting plasma cells, lymphocytes, macrophages, eosinophils, fenestrated capillaries and lymphatics, forming the diffuse part of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT). In a section, it appears as a loose, pinkish stroma with many scattered cells, forming the cores of the villi and surrounding the crypts.

The villus lamina propria core is the loose connective tissue at the centre of each villus, a finger-like fold of mucosa projecting into the lumen. It holds a central lacteal, a blind-ended lymphatic vessel that takes up dietary fat as chylomicrons, and a fenestrated capillary network that absorbs sugars and amino acids. Strands of smooth muscle running up the core shorten the villus, which helps empty the lacteal. In a section, the core is the pale connective-tissue stroma beneath the epithelium.

Central lacteals are the blind-ended lymphatic capillaries that run up the middle of each villus. Enterocytes release chylomicrons, made from dietary fat, into the lamina propria, and the lacteals take them up and drain them into the submucosal lymphatic plexus. In a section, they are small, pale central channels with a thin endothelial lining and few or no red blood cells.

The villus capillary network is the dense mesh of fenestrated capillaries just beneath the epithelium of each villus, surrounding the central lacteal. These capillaries take up sugars and amino acids and carry them to the liver through the hepatic portal vein. Their fenestrations, which are pores in the endothelium, let absorbed nutrients pass quickly into the blood. In a section, they appear as many small channels packed with red blood cells.

Villus smooth muscle is the bundle of smooth muscle fibres that runs up the core of each villus, arising from the muscularis mucosae at the base. Its contraction shortens the villus and helps squeeze the central lacteal, moving fat-rich lymph onward. In a section, look for elongated, spindle-shaped nuclei running along the axis of the villus core, between the lacteal and the capillaries.

Peyer's patch follicles are the rounded nodules of lymphoid tissue that make up Peyer's patches in the ileal wall. They sit in the lamina propria and extend into the submucosa, mostly on the antimesenteric side of the ileum, and are packed with B lymphocytes that respond to antigens from the gut lumen. In a section, they show as dense, dark-staining nodules of lymphocytes, often with a pale germinal centre.

Germinal centres are the paler, central zones of an active Peyer's patch follicle, where B cells multiply rapidly. Here B cells make small changes to their antibody genes and switch to making IgA, and those with the best-fitting antibodies mature into plasma cells or memory cells. In a section, the centre looks lighter than the dark ring of surrounding lymphocytes, and it holds dividing cells and macrophages that clear dead cells.

The subepithelial dome is the region of a Peyer's patch lying directly beneath the follicle-associated epithelium, the lining over the patch that has no villi. It is packed with dendritic cells, macrophages and lymphocytes, and it receives antigens that M cells carry across the epithelium. In a section, it appears as a cell-dense zone just under the thin lining, where gut antigens are presented to immune cells.

Villus goblet cells are the mucus-secreting cells scattered among the enterocytes of the villus lining. They make mucin, a glycoprotein that forms a slippery protective layer over the epithelium and traps particles and microbes. In a section they look like wine-glass shapes, with a pale, mucus-filled top and a small basal nucleus, and they stain strongly with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and Alcian blue.

Villus nuclei are the nuclei of the epithelial cells lining each villus, mainly enterocytes with some goblet cells. In the tall enterocytes the nucleus lies in the lower half of the cell, so the nuclei form a regular row through the lower part of the lining. In a section, they look like oval, blue-purple nuclei lined up in that row, a useful landmark for identifying the villus epithelium.

Villus mucin is the mucus secreted by the goblet cells of the villus, a gel of large glycoproteins called mucins that coats the epithelial surface. This layer lubricates the passage of digested food, traps particles and bacteria and helps protect the enterocytes from the contents of the lumen. Because it is often lost during routine slide preparation, it is best seen in sections stained with PAS or Alcian blue.

Villus enterocytes are the tall absorptive cells that make up most of the villus lining. Their apical surface bears a brush border of microvilli, which greatly enlarge the surface for absorbing digested sugars, amino acids, peptides and fatty acids. Neighbouring enterocytes are joined by tight junctions that stop luminal contents passing between them. In a section, they are tall columnar cells with a pink (eosinophilic) brush border and oval nuclei in a basal row.

The villus apical surface is the free, luminal border of the enterocytes lining each villus, and it is fringed with a brush border of microvilli. Enzymes such as sucrase-isomaltase and peptidases are embedded in the microvillus membrane, where they finish digesting sugars and peptides just before absorption. In a section, the apical border shows as a dense, pink, striped band along the luminal edge of the epithelium.

Villus enterocytes are the absorptive cells of the villus lining, and they are constantly renewed. Each one is born from a stem cell in the crypt, moves up the villus over about 3 to 5 days, and is shed from the tip into the lumen. In a section, it is a tall column with a striated brush border at its top and an oval nucleus low in the cell.

Villus nuclei are the nuclei of the absorptive enterocytes and goblet cells that line each villus. Because the villus lining is a single layer of tall columnar cells, the nuclei sit in one neat row towards the base of each cell and stain dark blue-purple in a haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) section. Goblet cells can be recognised among them by their nuclei, which are squeezed to the base beneath a pale, mucin-filled upper part of the cell.

The villus apical surface is the free border of the absorptive enterocytes that faces the gut lumen, and it is fringed by a dense brush border of microvilli. Each microvillus is a tiny finger-like extension of the cell membrane, and together they greatly increase the surface area available for absorbing digested nutrients. In a haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) section the brush border appears as a bright pink, striated band along the luminal edge of the villus, a useful clue for recognising absorptive cells.

Villus goblet cells are the mucus-producing cells that lie scattered among the absorptive enterocytes along the sides and tips of the villi. Each is flask-shaped, with a pale, mucin-filled upper part and a dark, flattened nucleus pushed to the base, so it stands out as a gap in the pink-fringed lining. Its secretion lubricates the villus surface and protects the lining from digestive juices and bacteria.

Villus mucin is the mucus secreted by the goblet cells on the villi. Mucin is a large glycoprotein, a protein heavily decorated with sugar chains, that absorbs water to form a slippery gel. In a section it stains magenta with the periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain and blue with Alcian blue, and it helps food slide past the lining while keeping bacteria at a distance.

Paneth cells are secretory epithelial cells found at the base of the intestinal crypts, the small glands between the villi, where they lie among the stem cells. Each is pyramid-shaped, with a round nucleus at the base and a cytoplasm packed with large, eosinophilic (pink-staining) granules in its upper part. These granules hold lysozyme and antimicrobial peptides called defensins, which help control bacteria in the gut, and in a haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) section their bright pink granules make them easy to spot.

Crypt nuclei are the nuclei of the epithelial cells that line each intestinal crypt, the narrow gland that opens between the villi. These cells include stem cells, Paneth cells and rapidly dividing transit cells that are on their way to becoming mature. The nuclei are round to oval, and dividing cells show dark, condensed chromosomes (mitotic figures), most often in the lower crypt.

Crypt granules are the secretory granules stored in the upper part of the Paneth cells at the base of the crypts. These membrane-bound granules are dense and strongly eosinophilic (pink-staining), and they contain lysozyme and defensins that are released into the crypt to kill bacteria. In a haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) section they give the crypt base a bright pink, grainy look that is quite distinctive.

Crypt stem cells are the unspecialised cells at the base of each intestinal crypt, sitting between the Paneth cells. They are small, narrow columnar cells with pale cytoplasm and oval nuclei, sitting at the very bottom of the crypt, where they divide constantly. Some of their daughter cells move up the crypt and mature into enteroendocrine (hormone-making) cells, enterocytes and goblet cells, while Paneth cells stay at the base; the whole lining is renewed about every 3 to 5 days.

Crypt enterocytes are young absorptive cells in the middle and lower crypt, just above the stem cells. They are columnar but shorter than mature villus enterocytes, and they lack many of their enzymes and features, while their brush border is shorter and sparser. As they climb towards the villus they mature into fully functional absorptive cells, and in a section their faint, indistinct brush border is a useful clue.

Crypt goblet cells are mucus-producing cells that lie scattered among the epithelial cells in the upper and middle crypt, above the stem cells. Like other goblet cells, they have a flask-shaped body with a pale, mucin-filled upper part and a dark nucleus at the base. Their mucus lubricates the crypt and helps protect it from bacteria and digestive secretions.

Crypt mucin is the mucus made by goblet cells inside the crypts, which is carried upwards to the surface of the gut. Mucin is a sugar-rich protein (a glycoprotein) that absorbs water and swells into a slippery gel. It stains magenta with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and blue with Alcian blue, and it forms a barrier that keeps gut bacteria away from the crypt epithelium.

Intervillus goblet cells are the mucus-secreting cells in the surface epithelium that lies between neighbouring villi, close to the openings of the crypts. This surface lining is a continuous sheet of simple columnar cells, with goblet cells scattered among them. Each goblet cell has a pale, mucin-filled upper part and a basal nucleus, and it releases mucus onto the surface to protect the mucosa.

Intervillus nuclei are the nuclei of the simple columnar cells that form the surface epithelium between neighbouring villi, extending down to the openings of the crypts. They are oval and lie in a neat row towards the base of each cell, staining dark purple in a haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) section. Because this surface is made of the same cell types as the villi, the nuclei are best recognised by where they lie, between adjacent villi, rather than by their look alone.

Intervillus mucin is the mucus poured onto the surface between neighbouring villi by the goblet cells of that surface. Mucin is a glycoprotein that swells into a slippery gel, lubricating the surface and trapping many bacteria before they reach the epithelium. In a section it turns bright magenta with the periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain, which is also used to show glycogen.

Intervillus enterocytes are the absorptive cells lining the surface epithelium between neighbouring villi, near the crypt openings. They are tall columnar cells with a brush border of microvilli on their free surface, and they absorb nutrients and water from the gut lumen. In a section, look for their tall, pink-fringed luminal border and oval basal nuclei, which set them apart from the paler goblet cells that sit among them.

FAE enterocytes are the absorptive cells of the follicle-associated epithelium (FAE), the thin, low lining over the dome of a Peyer's patch, a cluster of lymphoid follicles in the ileal wall. They are shorter and more cuboidal than villus enterocytes, and their brush border is sparser and shorter. Because this surface has no villi, it looks flatter than the rest of the ileal lining, and this flat outline is a useful clue in a section.

FAE nuclei are the nuclei of the cells in follicle-associated epithelium (FAE), the thin, low lining over the dome of a Peyer's patch in the ileum, where there are no villi. Because these cells are low and cuboidal, their round nuclei sit nearer the middle of each cell than the basal nuclei of tall villus enterocytes. Small dark lymphocyte nuclei are often seen pushing in among them, which helps to recognise this lining in a section.

Pocket lymphocytes are small immune cells (lymphocytes) that lie in the follicle-associated epithelium of a Peyer's patch, nestled in pockets of M cells (specialised cells that carry antigens across the lining). Each pocket is formed by the basal membrane of an M cell, folding inward to hold lymphocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells. The lymphocytes there receive antigens that the M cells carry across from the gut lumen. In a section, look for small, round, very dark nuclei sitting between or beneath the epithelial cells.

M cells, or microfold cells, are specialised epithelial cells of the follicle-associated epithelium (FAE) that line the dome of a Peyer's patch. They have few, short and irregular microvilli, and their basal membrane forms a pocket that holds lymphocytes and macrophages. M cells take up bacteria and antigens from the gut lumen by transcytosis (transport through the cell) and hand them to the immune cells in the pocket, so they are a key link between the gut and the lymphoid tissue.

Lying over the lymphoid nodules of a Peyer's patch in the ileum, FAE enterocytes are the absorptive cells of the follicle-associated epithelium (FAE). Compared with villus enterocytes, these cells are lower and more cuboidal, and their microvilli are fewer and shorter. Their job is still to absorb nutrients, but here they lie directly on top of the immune tissue beneath them.

FAE nuclei belong to the epithelial cells of the follicle-associated epithelium (FAE), the thin lining of cells that overlies a Peyer's patch in the ileum. The nuclei are round to oval and sit in a low, single layer alongside M cells (specialised cells that carry antigens across the lining) and absorptive enterocytes. Small dark lymphocyte nuclei are frequently seen between them, which helps to recognise this lining in a section.

Peyer's patch follicle nuclei are the nuclei of the lymphocytes (immune white blood cells) that pack the lymphoid follicles of the ileal wall. The nuclei are small, round and very dark, because they belong to small, densely packed lymphocytes, mainly B cells. In a haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) section a follicle therefore looks like a dark, crowded mass of nuclei.

Germinal centre nuclei are the nuclei of the B cells in the pale germinal centre at the heart of an active Peyer's patch follicle. Larger, paler nuclei belong to dividing B cells called centroblasts, while smaller, indented nuclei belong to centrocytes, which are being selected for higher-affinity antibodies. Scattered tingible body macrophages, which contain engulfed fragments of dead cells, are also present.

Subepithelial dome nuclei are the nuclei of the cells in the subepithelial dome, the loosely packed area of lymphoid tissue just beneath the follicle-associated epithelium of a Peyer's patch. This region holds a mixture of small lymphocyte nuclei and larger, paler nuclei of macrophages and dendritic cells (cells that present antigens to lymphocytes). Because the dome is less densely packed than a follicle, its nuclei look more spread out and less crowded.
